newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN MINISTER QUITS, ATTACKS GOVT ON ECONOMY.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN MINISTER QUITS, ATTACKS GOVT ON ECONOMY.

text.p: Bulgaria's Foreign Minister Georgi Pirinski, a prominent critic of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov, resigned on Wednesday saying the ruling Socialists did not have enough support to carry out the necessary economic reforms.

His resignation came a day after Videnov won a narrow victory over his Socialist party critics in a confidence vote and puts him in a strong position to challenge the premier at a party congress scheduled for December 21 and 22.
At the end of a marathon 20-hour meeting on Tuesday, 87 members of the party leadership backed Videnov in a confidence vote, 69 voted against him and two abstained.
Three members of the party's executive bureau resigned at the meeting, including vice chairman Yanaki Stoilov.
"The government lacks the minimum of public confidence it needs to carry out necessary economic policies," Pirinski told a news conference.
The pro-Western reformist Pirinski is often cited as a potential challenger to Videnov for the prime minister's job.
"I will work for the preparation of the extraordinary congress and I will fulfil my obligations as a politician," he said.
The opposition says it will press for early parliamentary elections in the hope of unseating the Socialists, who are half way through their four-year term.
The Constitutional Court barred Pirinski, a multi-lingual economist and experienced politician, from running for the presidency in elections last month because he was born in the United States.
The Socialists then picked Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, whose resounding defeat widened rifts within the party and prompted fresh calls for policy reforms and a new cabinet.

Pirinski said first deputy foreign minister Irina Bokova, who is responsible for relations with the European Union, would replace him temporarily and he had proposed her to Videnov as a permanent replacement.
Bokova ran for the vice-presidency on a joint ticket with Marazov.
The party plenum backed Videnov's support for a currency board proposed by the International Monetary Fund to halt the collapse of the Bulgarian currency and stabilise the economy.

The lev, which started the year at 70 to the dollar, fell to 260 on Wednesday. The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions plans a one-day general strike on December 4 to protest against falling living standards.

Pirinski accused the Socialist party of failing to carry out coherent economic reform in the past two years, saying the government and international financial institutions had so far failed to control the crisis,
"There is a need for a new package of stabilisation measures and for urgent measures to prevent the collapse of the financial system," he said.

The IMF has twice postponed a badly-needed $115 million credit due to Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets which include curbing inflation, stabilising the exchange rate, speeding up privatisation and closing loss-making enterprises.
Agreement with the Fund is vital if the Balkan state is to avoid defaulting on its $10 billion foreign debt.
